title: Ultrasonic Testing for LNG Facilities | UT Inspection (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic testing for US LNG terminals and liquefaction plants: piping thickness, cryogenic weld UT and tank checks to API 620. Request a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for LNG Facilities in the United States
html:
Atlantis NDT performs on-site ultrasonic testing (UT) for United States LNG facilities: thickness surveys on process and utility piping, weld examination on cryogenic tank and piping joints, and wall-loss checks on pretreatment, flare and boil-off systems. Technicians are mobilized to the terminal or liquefaction site, and the report names the procedure, equipment, calibration and every reading. To scope a job, request a UT inspection quote with your drawings and the governing code.

Where UT is used across an LNG facility

An LNG plant is two different metallurgical worlds sharing one fence. Upstream of the cold box, the feed gas passes through inlet separation, acid gas removal, dehydration and mercury removal. That service is carbon steel and low-alloy piping and vessels, with amine, glycol and condensate damage mechanisms that look much like a gas plant. Downstream of the cold box, everything runs at cryogenic temperature: refrigerant loops, the main exchangers, liquid transfer lines, storage tanks and the loading arms.

UT earns its place in both halves, but for different jobs. In the warm section it is mostly thickness work: circuits on amine regeneration, rich-amine lines, condensate and produced-water drains, flare headers and utility steam. In the cold section it is mostly weld and base-metal examination during construction, modification and repair, because thickness loss is rare in clean cryogenic service while weld quality governs whether a joint can take thermal cycling.

The US regulatory frame that drives the examination

US LNG facilities sit under several overlapping authorities, and the inspection scope usually traces back to one of them. The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration regulates onshore LNG plants under 49 CFR Part 193, which adopts NFPA 59A for design, construction, and operation of LNG facilities. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission authorizes and oversees siting and construction of export and import terminals, and its conditions often cite the same codes. The Coast Guard regulates waterfront transfer, and OSHA process safety management applies to the hazardous inventories on site.

Within those rules, the construction codes set the acceptance criteria. Storage tanks are built to API 620 (Appendix Q covers low-pressure tanks in refrigerated service) or API 625 for tank systems for refrigerated liquefied gas. Piping follows ASME B31.3, with cryogenic service requirements for materials and weld examination. For in-service piping the owner typically applies API 570 and the inspection program set by its own integrity engineers. Atlantis does not set intervals or calculate remaining life; the owner's engineer or authorized inspector uses our data for that.

Thickness surveys on the warm side

Ultrasonic thickness testing is the workhorse for pretreatment and utility systems. A typical survey uses a corrosion-grade dual-element probe on carbon steel, calibrated on a step block of the same material and checked against a known thickness before and after each circuit. Readings are taken at defined condition monitoring locations marked on the isometric, with enough grid density at elbows, tees, reducers and low points to catch localized loss. Where the owner's program uses condition monitoring locations, we record to those IDs so the trend line stays continuous from one outage to the next.

Amine units deserve extra attention. Rich-amine piping downstream of the absorber, and the regenerator overhead, are classic locations for localized corrosion where velocity, temperature or heat-stable salts concentrate. A grid on the outside of the pipe, taken after surface cleaning, shows the pattern; a single spot reading would not. Flare headers and knockout drum shells collect wet, acidic condensate, and their low points are scanned on a fixed grid for the same reason. Surface temperature matters: standard couplant and probes work to the limits in the procedure, and hot lines call for high-temperature couplant and a velocity correction or a shutdown window.

Weld examination in cryogenic construction and repair

Shear-wave UT of welds is performed to a written procedure that follows ASME Section V Article 4, with the scan plan, reference reflectors and recording thresholds taken from the construction code or the owner's specification. The material decides how much the procedure has to adapt. Austenitic stainless piping (304L, 316L) has coarse, directional grain in the weld metal that scatters and bends sound, so a procedure for these joints is demonstrated on a representative mock-up before it is used on the line. The same is true of nickel-alloy filler metal used to weld 9% nickel steel tanks.

9% nickel steel is the standard inner-tank material for full-containment and single-containment LNG tanks, chosen for toughness at about minus 260 degrees Fahrenheit. Its plate welds are made with nickel-based filler, and the weld zone attenuates sound more than carbon steel does. Where a specification allows UT in place of other volumetric methods, the owner's Level III and engineer decide whether the demonstrated technique meets that allowance. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, so on projects that require it, the owner uses a licensed radiography contractor and we work the UT, magnetic particle and penetrant scope around it.

Because the right answer changes by material, the two siblings of this page are worth reading alongside it: magnetic particle testing for LNG explains why MT stops at the stainless boundary, and liquid penetrant testing for LNG covers surface-breaking flaws on every metal in the plant.

Technique details that matter in cold-service work

Several habits keep UT results defensible in an LNG setting. Calibration blocks match the material: stainless and nickel-alloy sound velocities differ from carbon steel, so a reading taken with a steel velocity on a stainless pipe is wrong by several percent and has to be corrected or recalibrated. Couplant is chosen for the surface temperature and, on cold lines in operation, for the frost and moisture present. Insulated cryogenic piping gets examined at the insulation windows the owner opens, because ice and wet insulation are the cold-service version of corrosion under insulation.

Surface preparation is specified in the procedure. Welds are examined with the crown conditioned as the code requires, and probe contact on thin-wall stainless needs a smooth, clean surface. Where plate laminations might interfere with an angle-beam scan, a straight-beam check of the scan area comes first. Sensitivity is set on reference reflectors in a block of the same product form, and the reference level is stated in the report so the owner can audit the decision.

What the UT report contains

The deliverable is built for the owner's integrity group and for an audit by the regulator or a third party. Each report carries:

  • Equipment tag, line or component ID, drawing reference, and exam date
  • Written procedure number and revision, and the code or specification governing acceptance
  • Instrument, probe, calibration block and couplant, with the calibration check results
  • Technician name and SNT-TC-1A level, and the Level III who approved the procedure
  • Thickness grids or scan sketches, with the minimum reading and its location marked
  • For welds, indication location, length, amplitude against the reference level, and accept or reject against the named criteria

Atlantis reports the data and flags indications; acceptance against the contract or code is decided by the owner's inspector or engineer, and any repair or fitness-for-service decision is theirs. That separation is deliberate and keeps our role clear in a regulated environment.

What to send for a UT quote

  • Isometrics, line list or CML list, or weld maps for the scope
  • Material, nominal wall thickness, diameter and operating temperature for each line or component
  • The governing code or specification and the acceptance criteria
  • Insulation and coating status, and who removes and restores it
  • Access arrangements: scaffold, lift, confined space, hot work and gas-test rules
  • Site address, badging and TWIC requirements, and the contact for permits

Planning realities at US LNG sites

LNG sites are secure and permit-heavy. Expect site orientation, gas monitoring, TWIC for access to waterfront areas, and work permits that can restrict ignition sources and cold-area entry. Outage windows are short and shared with mechanical crews, so a thickness scope is sequenced behind insulation removal and scaffolding. Coastal weather in the Gulf and the Southeast also affects scheduling: wind limits for lifts, heat, and lightning stops. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and we ask for the safety orientation schedule up front so it does not eat inspection time.

Where we work in the US for LNG

  • Corpus Christi: liquefaction and export infrastructure on the south Texas coast, with long welded pipe racks and marine transfer lines.
  • Lake Charles: the Calcasieu Ship Channel corridor in Louisiana, where large liquefaction and export facilities and a dense refining base share contractors.
  • Beaumont: the Sabine-Neches area of Texas, close to the Sabine Pass export terminals and the petrochemical plants that supply the region.
  • Houston: the largest pool of fabrication shops and engineering firms serving Gulf Coast LNG, including module and spool work before it ships.
  • Savannah: the Elba Island LNG terminal area on the Georgia coast, an import and small-scale liquefaction site.
  • Baltimore: the Chesapeake Bay region, home to the Cove Point terminal in Maryland, which handles both import history and export.

Training your own UT technicians

Owners that build their own inspection groups can start with our online theory and simulator practice. See UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with practice time on the ultrasonic testing simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel, so the course supports the employer's written practice; it does not replace it. Procedure writing and qualification are covered under NDT procedure development.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not run in-line inspection tools, and does not offer the specialist techniques that sit outside this page. We also do not calculate remaining life or set inspection intervals, and we do not hold nuclear quality-program qualifications. If your LNG scope includes one of those, we will say so at the quote stage and work around it. For national background see ultrasonic testing services and the UT guide.

faq.q: Can UT be used on 9% nickel steel LNG tanks?
faq.a: Yes, for base metal thickness and for plate and weld examination, provided the procedure accounts for the material. Weld metal made with nickel-based filler is coarse-grained, so the technique is demonstrated on a representative block and the owner decides whether it meets the specification.

faq.q: Which codes govern UT at a US LNG terminal?
faq.a: PHMSA 49 CFR Part 193 and NFPA 59A set the facility framework, API 620 and API 625 cover the tanks, and ASME B31.3 covers process piping. ASME Section V sets the UT method, and the owner picks the acceptance criteria.

faq.q: Does cryogenic service change how thickness is measured?
faq.a: The method is the same, but stainless and nickel alloys have different sound velocities than carbon steel, so the instrument is calibrated on a matching block. Frost, moisture and insulation also affect couplant choice and access.

faq.q: Can you inspect while the plant is running?
faq.a: Thickness surveys on accessible lines can often be done in operation if surface temperature, permits and safe access allow. Weld examination and anything under insulation usually waits for a shutdown or a planned insulation window.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects indications on LNG welds?
faq.a: Our technician records and reports the indications against the named criteria, and the owner's inspector or engineer makes the acceptance and repair decision. An ASNT Level III reviews our procedure and reports.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote a UT thickness survey?
faq.a: Isometrics or a condition monitoring location list, material and nominal thickness, operating temperature, insulation status, access method, site address and any badging or TWIC requirements. A line list is enough to start.

faq.q: Do you provide radiography for LNG projects in the US?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States because industrial radiography is licensed under federal and state radiation rules. We handle the UT, magnetic particle and penetrant scope and coordinate with your licensed contractor.

Technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: Is UT or PT better for a final check on stainless piping welds?
faq.a: They find different things. UT sees internal volumetric flaws and measures wall thickness, while penetrant testing finds surface-breaking flaws on the finished weld surface. Many cryogenic specifications call for both.
